newsitem.title: USA: U.S. general is unlikely victim of morals uproar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. general is unlikely victim of morals uproar.

text.p: U.S. Air Force General Joseph Ralston, who survived 147 missions over Laos and Vietnam, is an unlikely figure to be sucked into the national uproar over morals in the military.

Ralston, 53, a combination of tough action man and soft-spoken leader and one of the military's quickest rising stars, was until about a week ago favoured to take over as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the military's top job.

The well-liked southerner, already vice-chairman of the Joint Chiefs, seemed a safe choice to fill the high-profile post General John Shalikashvili is due to vacate Sept. 30 and which Colin Powell held during the 1991 Gulf War.

But the rosy picture darkened when, amid an emotional debate on whether double standards were applied to different ranks and sexes in imposing military codes of ethics, it was disclosed that Ralston himself had had an adulterous affair.

Initially Defence Secretary William Cohen indicated the affair, which happened more than a decade ago, would not block his rise to the top. But outrage among some politicians and social groups prompted them, and Ralston, to think again.

A highly decorated Vietnam War veteran, Ralston had been vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs since March 1, 1996 and his term expires at the end of next February. He won respect from fellow military leaders and political leaders.
"I relied heavily on his keen judgment and leadership during my time as secretary of defence," said William Perry, who presided over the Pentagon during President Clinton's first term.

Ralston recently played a central role in the Pentagon's Quadrennial Defence Review, a formal assessment of missions, strategies and weapons carried out every four years. His reputation was that of a middle-of-the-road consensus builder.
He also had held a major command, Air Force Air Combat, where he was responsible for training and equipping all combat operations in the United States.
Ralston's past caught up with him while he was visiting former Soviet republics in Central Asia last week.

Responding to newspaper queries, Defence Secretary William Cohen called to ask if he had ever committed adultery. Ralston admitted he had had an affair for about a year with a civilian woman while he was estranged from his wife 13 years ago.

The affair began while the general and the woman, an analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency, were students at the Pentagon's National War College. Ralston was separated from his wife at the time and they divorced in 1988.
Caspar Weinberger, defence secretary under President Ronald Reagan in the 1980s, is among many who have worked with him who praise him for his fine record.

"I think it's very unfortunate that the country would lose the services of an officer of this standing and character," Weinberger said Sunday in a television interview amid reports that Ralston's career was doomed.
"He's had a heroic record in Vietnam and elsewhere and he's a superb officer. And I think he would make a very fine chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff," Weinberger said.
Joseph W. Ralston was born in Hopkinsville, Kentucky on Nov. 4, 1943. He entered the Air Force in 1965 through the Reserve Officer Training Programme.
Ralston had two children by his first wife. His second wife, the former Diane Dougherty, whom he married in 1989, had two children of her own.
